questions.question_text:
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^{3}+2t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(5t^{2}-t)\underset{\sim}{j}$.
Which vector is $\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$?

options.why: Differentiated $5t^{2}$ correctly but left the $-t$ term in the j component undifferentiated.
Differentiated $t^{3}$ correctly but left the $+2t$ term in the i component undifferentiated.
Differentiated only the highest power in each component and copied the remaining term across.

questions.question_text:
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(2t^{4}-t^{2})\underset{\sim}{i}+(t^{3}+4t)\underset{\sim}{j}$.
Which vector is $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)$?

options.why: Differentiated the j component only once, so that entry is still a velocity component.
Differentiated the i component only once, so that entry is still a velocity component.
Stopped after one differentiation and gave $\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$ instead of $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)$.

questions.question_text:
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^{2}-6t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(t^{3}+t)\underset{\sim}{j}$.
What is its velocity when $t=4$?

options.why: Substituted $t=4$ into $y(t)$ instead of $\dot{y}(t)$ for the j component.
Substituted $t=4$ into $x(t)$ instead of $\dot{x}(t)$ for the i component.
Substituted into the position vector and gave $\underset{\sim}{r}(4)$ rather than the velocity.

questions.question_text:
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=2t^{2}\underset{\sim}{i}+15t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$.
What is its speed when $t=2$?

options.why: Added $\dot{x}$ and $\dot{y}$ instead of using $\sqrt{\dot{x}^{2}+\dot{y}^{2}}$.
Added the components first and then took the square root, instead of adding their squares.
Worked out $\dot{x}^{2}+\dot{y}^{2}$ correctly but forgot to take the square root.

questions.question_text:
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=5\cos 4t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+5\sin 4t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$.
Which statement about its motion is correct?

options.text: The speed is constant at $20$, and the acceleration is always perpendicular to the velocity.
The speed is constant at $5$, and the acceleration is always perpendicular to the velocity.
options.why: Quoted the radius $5$ as the speed instead of computing $|\underset{\sim}{v}|=\sqrt{400\sin^{2}4t+400\cos^{2}4t}=20$.

options.text: The speed is constant at $20$, and the acceleration always points in the same direction as the velocity.
options.why: Assumed acceleration must act along the direction of motion; here $\underset{\sim}{v}\cdot\underset{\sim}{a}=0$.

options.text: The speed is constant at $5$, and the acceleration always points in the same direction as the velocity.
options.why: Used the radius as the speed and also assumed acceleration acts along the direction of motion.

questions.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$
$=-20\sin 4t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+20\cos 4t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$
$|\underset{\sim}{v}(t)|$
$=\sqrt{400\sin^{2}4t+400\cos^{2}4t}$
$=20$
$\underset{\sim}{a}(t)$
$=-80\cos 4t\,\underset{\sim}{i}-80\sin 4t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$
$\underset{\sim}{v}\cdot\underset{\sim}{a}$
$=1600\sin 4t\cos 4t-1600\sin 4t\cos 4t$
$=0$
The speed is constant at $20$ and the acceleration is perpendicular to the velocity.

questions.question_text:
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=e^{3t}\underset{\sim}{i}+\sin 2t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$.
Which vector is $\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$?

options.why: Attached the minus sign from the derivative of cosine to the derivative of $\sin 2t$.
Left out the chain-rule factor of $3$ when differentiating $e^{3t}$.
Omitted the chain-rule factor on the exponential and used the wrong sign on the sine derivative.

questions.question_text:
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^{4}-2t^{3})\underset{\sim}{i}+t^{5}\underset{\sim}{j}$.
What is $\underset{\sim}{a}(1)$?

options.why: Differentiated the j component once instead of twice, giving $\dot{y}(1)=5$.
Differentiated the i component once instead of twice, giving $\dot{x}(1)=-2$.
Gave $\underset{\sim}{v}(1)$ instead of $\underset{\sim}{a}(1)$.

questions.question_text:
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^{2}-8t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(t^{2}+6t)\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge 0$.
At what time is the particle moving in a direction parallel to $\underset{\sim}{i}+3\underset{\sim}{j}$?

options.why: Solved $2t+6=3(2t-8)$ but expanded the right side as $6t-8$, forgetting to multiply the $-8$ by $3$.
Found when $\dot{x}=0$, which gives motion parallel to $\underset{\sim}{j}$, rather than matching the given direction.
Made the position vector parallel to $\underset{\sim}{i}+3\underset{\sim}{j}$ instead of the velocity vector.

questions.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$
$=(2t-8)\underset{\sim}{i}+(2t+6)\underset{\sim}{j}$
For $\underset{\sim}{v}$ parallel to $\underset{\sim}{i}+3\underset{\sim}{j}$, the j component must be $3$ times the i component.
$2t+6=3(2t-8)$
$2t+6=6t-24$
$30=4t$
$t=7.5$
Check: $\underset{\sim}{v}(7.5)=7\underset{\sim}{i}+21\underset{\sim}{j}=7\left(\underset{\sim}{i}+3\underset{\sim}{j}\right)$.
